story.title: The Man Who Measured Dawn: How Saleh Al-Saleh Built Oman's First Modern Hijri Calendar
story.seo_title: Saleh Al-Saleh: Maker of Oman's First Modern Hijri Calendar
story.meta_description: Discover the life of late Omani astronomer Saleh bin Ubaid Al-Saleh, the self-taught scholar who calculated Oman's first modern Hijri calendar in 1979.

detail.extracted_title: The Man Who Measured Dawn: How Saleh Al-Saleh Built Oman's First Modern Hijri Calendar
detail.excerpt: Standing behind the coastal cliffs of Al-Bustan at three in the morning in the late 1970s, self-taught Omani astronomer Saleh bin Ubaid Al-Saleh charted the solar and lunar cycles that produced the Sultanate's first modern Hijri and agricultural calendars.
detail.article_html:
Long before satellite clocks and automated astronomical software standardized prayer times across the Arabian Peninsula, a single man stood in the pre-dawn darkness behind the coastal mountains of Al-Bustan in Muscat, watching the eastern horizon at three in the morning. For three consecutive mornings, Saleh bin Ubaid Al-Saleh tracked the first break of light over the Gulf of Oman. He then traveled north to Wilayat Saham on the Al-Batinah coast and spent three evenings recording the exact moment the sun dropped below the western horizon. From those field observations, paired with classical calculations of solar declinations and lunar mansions, he mapped the minute-by-minute time differentials across the wilayats of the Sultanate.

On Tuesday evening, Oman lost one of its last traditional astronomical calculators when Saleh bin Ubaid Al-Saleh passed away after decades of quiet service to the nation's scientific and agricultural heritage. Mourned by the Omani Society for Astronomy and Space and generations of researchers, Al-Saleh leaves behind an extraordinary legacy: the preparation of the first modern Omani Hijri calendar issued in the name of the Sultanate of Oman in 1400 AH (1979 CE).

A Self-Taught Scholar of the Skies

Unlike university-trained astrophysicists of later decades, Al-Saleh built his mastery of celestial mechanics through relentless personal inquiry. His formal education began in 1958 when he enrolled at Qatar Model Primary School. His early travels took him between Qatar and Egypt, where he sought out classical treatises, astronomical tables, and seasoned scholars. Although he never pursued a specialized university degree in astronomy, he mastered the intricate mathematics of the skies through independent reading, observation, and calculation.

In Omani tradition, the hasib—the astronomical calculator—occupied a vital civic role, bridging maritime navigation, seasonal agriculture, and religious timekeeping. Al-Saleh carried this classical discipline into the modern state era. Working with modest instruments and handwritten tables, he relied on his command of the rising and setting of the southern star Suhayl (Canopus), the twelve zodiacal constellations (manazil al-buruj), and the twenty-eight lunar mansions (manazil al-qamar). In a previous interview reflecting on his life's work, Al-Saleh noted that despite the scarcity of technical equipment in those early years, his published calculations never recorded a single timing error.

The 1400 AH Milestone: Unifying Time Across the Wilayats

As Oman's modern institutions expanded during the late 1970s, the Ministry of Justice, Awqaf and Islamic Affairs needed an authoritative national calendar tailored specifically to Oman's varied topography and longitudes. In 1400 AH (1979 CE), Al-Saleh prepared the first modern Hijri calendar bearing the name of the Sultanate of Oman.

The task required exceptional precision. At the time, many Omani communities still referenced two distinct timekeeping conventions: ghuroobi time, an older Arabian system in which the daily clock resets at sunset, and zawali (meridian) time, the standard modern system anchored to solar noon and midnight. Al-Saleh calculated prayer timetables across Omani wilayats in both the ghuroobi and zawali systems, allowing mosque imams, judges, and citizens from Muscat to the interior and coastal provinces to transition smoothly while maintaining exact adherence to local solar positions.

Charting the Seasons for Farmers and UNESCO

Al-Saleh recognized that the movement of the stars governed life on the soil just as much as it marked the hours of prayer. Drawing on centuries of Omani agronomic wisdom, he compiled a comprehensive agricultural calendar (taqwim zira'i) that correlated celestial cycles with the optimal windows for planting, pollinating, and harvesting crops across Oman's diverse microclimates.

That agricultural calendar remains preserved today at the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources as a foundational reference on indigenous seasonal knowledge. Recognizing its cultural and scientific value, officials also dispatched a copy of Al-Saleh's agricultural calendar to the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), documenting how Omani calculators harmonized farming cycles with stellar and lunar movements.

From the rocky coastline of Al-Bustan to the date groves of Saham, Saleh bin Ubaid Al-Saleh proved that scientific rigor begins with patience, observation, and an enduring devotion to the land and sky. Every daily prayer timetable and Hijri calendar printed in the Sultanate today stands on the foundation he calculated by hand nearly half a century ago.

detail.instagram_caption:
In the late 1970s, before satellite clocks and digital software standardized prayer timetables across the region, Saleh bin Ubaid Al-Saleh stood in the dark behind the coastal mountains of Al-Bustan in Muscat at 3:00 AM. For three consecutive mornings, he tracked the exact break of dawn over the sea, then traveled north to Wilayat Saham for three days to record sunset differentials across Oman's coastline.

On Tuesday evening, Oman bid farewell to the self-taught astronomical calculator who prepared the first modern Hijri calendar in the name of the Sultanate of Oman in 1400 AH (1979 CE). Beginning his schooling in 1958 and educating himself through travels in Qatar and Egypt, Al-Saleh mastered the movements of the star Suhayl, the zodiacal constellations, and the 28 lunar mansions. He calculated prayer times for Omani wilayats across both the traditional ghuroobi (sunset) and modern zawali (meridian) systems without a single recorded error, and compiled a landmark agricultural calendar preserved at the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources and shared with UNESCO.

How do we preserve the legacy of self-taught Omani scholars who bridged traditional science and modern institutions?
